source.title: Interpreting the Second-Order Effects of Neurons in CLIP
source.authors: Yossi Gandelsman; Alexei A. Efros; Jacob Steinhardt

record.tranche_reason: Tests neuron polysemanticity in CLIP using second-order effects and sparse text decompositions, a different measurement from the original sources.
record.gate_note: Rows record the separately reported neuron decompositions in Tables 2 and 5. Layer-ablation, reconstruction-accuracy, adversarial-image, and segmentation results are not rows here because they do not directly measure whether individual neurons have multiple meanings. The cited results from prior work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study checks whether individual CLIP ViT-B-32 vision neurons correspond to multiple concepts. It uses sparse text decompositions of each neuron's second-order output direction and looks at its top-effect images. This is a new model class and method for V1. It reports no share of neurons and does not test causes or alternative explanations.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors find CLIP neurons' second-order effects are sparse (significant for under 2% of images) and roughly rank-1. Text decompositions of these effects show polysemantic neurons spanning multiple, often unrelated concepts, which the authors present as corroborating prior superposition literature rather than testing it. They exploit this for semantic adversarial images and zero-shot segmentation.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a second-order effect through later attention heads and sparse decomposition into text representations, rather than the original sources' neuron-visualization or circuit analyses.
record.method_sensitivity: Text-pool type and decomposition set size affect reconstruction accuracy; the paper reports that larger description sets approach the original classification accuracy and that full descriptions outperform single words at smaller set sizes.
record.problems: Polysemanticity evidence is primarily qualitative examples from sparse decompositions, not a measured fraction of neurons. The reported examples are from CLIP ViT layer 9 and do not establish how common the phenomenon is across models. The authors also note that their analysis omits neuron effects on attention queries and keys and interactions between neurons.
record.rows_left_out: Table 5 neuron #2002 is omitted because the flattened table text does not clearly assign all displayed descriptions and words to that neuron. Other neuron examples in Figures 13–14 are not separately recorded because the paper does not provide their concept descriptions there. Layer ablations, reconstruction accuracy, adversarial attacks, and segmentation comparisons are omitted because they do not directly measure polysemanticity.

untested.parts: Supervised image classifiers such as InceptionV1 are not studied. The evidence is from CLIP ViT-B-32 layer 9 only, using hand-picked examples with no frequency reported.
The authors invoke superposition only by citing Elhage et al.; they do not test it as a cause.
No tests of initialization, regularization or training noise.
No comparison of activation functions, architectures or training choices.
The study does not examine whether the mixed concepts reduce to one shared feature, and gives no frequency of truly unrelated mixtures.
No comparison of activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods. Decomposition size and text pool are varied only for reconstruction accuracy.

missing.what: Top images by second-order-effect norm for each neuron. The paper says these show multiple concepts (cars and boats), and that more concepts appear among the top 50. This is the response-based evidence closest to V1.
Table 5 neuron #2002: positive terms sustainable living, train yard, rescue equipment, governance, gravel, conserve; negative terms snow-covered rooftops, genres.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche set to T3 (new model class, CLIP ViT) rather than T2. The decompositions describe what a neuron writes toward (its output direction), not what inputs activate it. Many listed terms have negative coefficients, and the reader treated them as co-detected concepts. Several showcased neurons (#4, #391, #2137) have positive terms sharing one theme, so they are weak evidence of unrelated mixtures. V6 links and the 'challenges' label were removed because the study does not test the shared-feature explanation. The evidence is qualitative, hand-picked examples from one layer of one model.

versions.untested_parts: The examples are from CLIP ViT models, not InceptionV1; the study interprets second-order effects rather than directly testing neuron responses.
No transformer language models or language-neuron polysemanticity are studied.
The study reports multiple concepts per neuron but does not test whether this is caused by representing more sparse features than there are neurons or by capacity pressure.
Initialization, regularization, training noise, and conditions with sufficient neurons are not tested as causes.
The study does not compare activation functions or regularization, or measure how the share of polysemantic neurons changes across architectures or training choices.
The study does not establish the population frequency of truly unrelated mixtures or systematically compare its interpretations with alternative explanations such as shared pose.
The study does not compare polysemanticity judgments across activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.

rows.subject: OpenAI's ViT-B-32 CLIP
rows.operation_detail: Sparse text decomposition of the neuron’s second-order-effect direction
rows.measure: Concepts in the top-4 text descriptions and their coefficient signs
rows.value: Descriptions include falling snow, extreme weather, a construction-site bucket, and a holiday service.
rows.note: The study presents these as examples of a neuron corresponding to multiple concepts.
rows.check: The positive terms (snowflakes, extreme weather, holiday service) share a winter theme. The construction-site bucket has a negative coefficient, so it is not a concept the neuron writes toward. Unlinked from V6: the study does not test whether the mixtures reduce to one feature.

relationships.condition: Selected CLIP ViT-B-32 layer-9 neurons whose positive-coefficient terms span distinct concepts
relationships.reason: Positive decomposition terms mix unrelated concepts: limousine/suit/bullmastiff, yacht/cabriolet/cirrus, runners/expiration, pedal/graffiti. Figure 5 top images also show cars and boats for one neuron.
relationships.display_finding: The neurons' positive decomposition terms combined unrelated concepts: limousine/suit/bullmastiff, yacht/cabriolet/cirrus, runners/expiration and pedal/graffiti. One neuron's top images showed both cars and boats.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Selected CLIP ViT-B-32 layer-9 neurons whose positive-coefficient terms span distinct concepts
source_check.reason: Hand-picked neurons such as #2914 have positive terms across cars, boats and animals, and the Figure 5 caption cites cars and boats. The evidence is qualitative and gives no share of neurons.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

labels.label: supports
labels.condition: Selected CLIP ViT-B-32 layer-9 neurons whose positive-coefficient terms span distinct concepts
labels.reason: Hand-picked neurons such as #2914 have positive terms across cars, boats and animals, and the Figure 5 caption cites cars and boats. The evidence is qualitative and gives no share of neurons.

relation.reason: The study's own decompositions (Tables 2 and 5) and top images (Figure 5) bear on V1. The abstract says the sets reveal neurons with multiple, often unrelated concepts. That is its own result, not just discussion.

tranche.reason: The study interprets CLIP ViT-B-32 neurons, a new model class compared with the CNN classifiers in V1. Polysemanticity is a by-product of that work, not the question it is aimed at, so T3 fits better than T2.

source_check.notes: Examples are hand-picked and qualitative, and no share of neurons is reported. #4, #391 and #2137 have positive terms that share a theme (winter, mostly wood, food/drink). Table 5 gives no layer or model; layer 9 of ViT-B-32 is inferred from the Table 2 caption. For #974 the signs conflict across pools (race descriptions negative, runners/races words positive), so splits by sign are fragile.

reader_labels.label: supports

reader_labels.reason: The decompositions for individual neurons contain multiple distinct concepts, including object and scene categories; see rows T2-4-desc through T5-1517-words.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Qualitative sparse-text interpretations of the reported ViT-B-32 CLIP neurons
reader_labels.reason: Several neurons are assigned concepts from distinct domains rather than one clearly shared feature; examples include the limousine, suit, celebrity, and dog descriptions for #2914 and the distinct concepts for #2137; see rows T2-2137-desc and T2-2914-desc.
